tips.text: Pin an order and it repeats every turn until you unpin it.
A turn can last a week or a whole year: pick its length before you end it.
A question to a minister changes nothing in the world: ask as much as you need before the turn.
In private a deputy speaks more frankly than their minister.
A minister who kept quiet after the turn will answer if you ask for their view in the cabinet.
The Chronicle tab downloads the whole game as text.
The Chronicle tab can play your whole game back as a timelapse of the map.
Any country is playable – in 1991 even a republic with no land of its own yet.
Other countries' figures are your government's estimates, not the truth.
Overthrown? The game goes on: go into opposition or play the new government.
Lost all your land? Your government carries on in exile.
Orders can be dictated: press the microphone in the order field.
The turn's report can be read to you aloud: the speaker next to its headline.
Click any country on the map to see its economy, army and alliances.
The map has modes – terrain, resources, population, transport – in the buttons at its bottom right.
Zoom in on the map to see the towns and the front running between them.
Drop a save file onto the front page to load it.
Money for science and education speeds up every other direction of research.
The military, intelligence and the interior ministry can plan a special operation – it starts only once you approve it.
A ministry's directive stays in force for several turns, until it is done or fails.
A minister you do not trust can be replaced: the cabinet finds candidates for every post.
A law changes by a vote in parliament or, where the regime allows, by decree.
Grain, oil, gas and arms can be sold or bought on contract in the Economy tab.
Foreign policy can call a summit or a session of an organisation your country belongs to.
The Crises chip in the top bar shows what is going wrong and what it will bring.
In the desktop app F11 switches between full screen and a window.
Ctrl+Enter adds the order you are typing – no need to reach for the button.
Click an order to change it: Enter saves, Shift+Enter starts a new line, Esc cancels.
Twelve orders a turn, standing ones included: keep the ones that matter.
Nothing written yet? One button repeats all of last turn's orders.
Last turn's orders wait under the field: “Edit and repeat” brings one back to change.
Concrete orders work best: what, where, how much. “Raise the income tax to 30%” beats “fix the economy”.
Every order gets a verdict in the report – done, partly or failed.
A turn without orders is allowed: things simply go on as they were.
Every minister has a character, ability, loyalty and interests of their own.
After a turn a minister may object in their report when you go against their causes.
At most twelve directives across the cabinet: give each ministry the one that matters.
A directive is a standing task: “raise the grain harvest by a fifth” keeps a ministry busy for turns.
Appointing a minister, you can name anyone at all, not only the candidates offered.
Ask for candidates with a wish: a loyalist, a technocrat, someone from the opposition.
Unsure about a candidate? Talk it over with an adviser before you appoint.
Change the budget, then approve it; Undo puts the old figures back.
The finance minister can propose a budget for you: read it, then apply it in one click.
A deficit is paid with debt or reserves, and interest climbs as debt grows against GDP.
Printed money, shortages and war push prices up; a tight budget brings them down.
Keep an eye on unrest: from 65 the government can be overthrown.
Unrest rises with war, poverty and prices, and falls with concessions and order.
Point at a figure in the top bar, or tap it, to see what moves it.
When the harvest fails, imports and grain contracts keep people fed – until the money runs out.
A blockade cuts the imports a country eats from: mind your supply before you start a war at sea.
Cutting social spending saves money and lowers supply – people notice.
New contracts are limited per turn: the Deals tab shows how many are left.
Research money is a fifth of the army budget and three tenths of industry's: cut those, and science slows.
Research runs in seven directions; a breakthrough comes when one reaches the year history made it.
With money and an able science minister a direction can run years ahead of history.
An atomic programme moves only with a minimum share of the research money.
“Learn about the army” has the game master describe your armies, fleets and air force.
“Order an offensive” writes an order for one army or the whole army: where, with what, by when.
New recruits are not soldiers yet: the Army tab lists those still in training apart.
Industry can build up to two kinds of weapons first, at twice the money.
Not sure what to build? Ask what the army needs most – the answer costs no game time.
Every war shows its losses – killed, wounded, equipment – and the enemy's as an intelligence estimate.
How well you know a country depends on alliances, borders, talks and your spies.
Closed regimes are hard to read: their figures come as ranges and rumours.
“Rumoured” means just that: your government has heard it, not seen it.
You can write to any government: pick the country in the list or on the map.
At a summit you can attend in person and speak for your government yourself.
During a meeting you can ask quietly what the others really want – they will not hear.
What is agreed at a meeting binds the next turn – as far as each side keeps its word.
You can found a bloc of your own and give it a name – a Black Sea League, say.
A session of an organisation is called by an order, like any other step.
A truce has an end date: Foreign policy shows until when it holds.
Every country has a foreign course: its aims, its plans in the open and what it remembers.
Wars rarely come from nowhere: tension, then preparation, show in a country's plans first.
Other countries show their risk of a coup – low, elevated or high, as a share a year.
In historical mode, what happened later is planned for its date – until you change the world.
In free mode the world goes its own way: wars and alliances grow out of each government's plans.
You can start in opposition: lead a party, or a movement underground where elections are not free.
In opposition you see the budget, the army and diplomacy but cannot change them: you push.
A motion shows how many votes it needs and how many the government has: count first.
The house votes after the government has spoken: open the sitting with your speech.
“Draft” has the interior minister write your words; you edit them and say them yourself.
No majority? Take a party into coalition, or buy its votes on one question – cheaper, but it names the price.
Below 40 loyalty orders to use force may be refused; below 25 units go over.
The police can stop a small protest; a big one comes back angrier.
Concessions calm the street at once but look weak – the hardliners will not forgive it.
Offering elections turns the street into a campaign – one you may lose.
A law you proclaim takes effect at the end of the turn.
Rename the country or a city, or change its colours: the weaker the case, the louder the outrage.
The Diplomacy map shows the allies, partners, enemies and pacts of any country you pick.
Layers switch rivers, railways, ports, cities, province borders and front lines on and off.
The “Changes in the turn” layer shows what moved on the map since the last turn.
Hatched land is occupied; the front runs through provinces, between the towns each side holds.
Point at a town to see its people, who holds it and whether a railway or a port serves it.
The Resources map shows who produces what in the game's year – and the largest producers.
Any turn can become a picture: its headline over a map of what changed, saved as PNG or copied.
The timelapse can be saved as a video – keep its tab in front while it records.
In the Chronicle any past turn can be shown on the map, with what it changed.
Rename a game on the front page; leave the name empty to go back to the country and year.
Copy a game on the front page to try another course without losing the first.
Dictation can run on your own computer: after a one-time download your voice goes nowhere.
The guided tour of the game can be replayed from Settings.
